look_here_first: RICE CUTGRASS (*Leersia oryzoides*). Look on STREAM EDGES/WET SOIL for an open loose panicle with small, FLAT, narrow rice-grain-shaped awnless spikelets. Next, using a lens rather than scraping your skin, look for BACKWARD-pointing minute stiff teeth/spinules along leaf edges and sheaths. For the look-alike WHITE CUTGRASS (*L. virginica*), inspect a WHOLE fully expanded panicle: rice cutgrass usually has TWO or more branches from its LOWEST branching nodes and longer mature spikelets ~4.2–6.5 mm. White cutgrass commonly has ONE lower branch and smaller ~2.2–4 mm spikelets; overlap exists. Check short true MEMBRANOUS ligule ~0.5–1 mm; one fertile floret per spikelet with NO conspicuous true glumes. These microscopic and low-node traits are not resolved in present photos.

best_field_traits: Long rhizomatous wetland perennial with spreading, often decumbent, rooted stems.
Rough leaf sheaths; blades often ~5–15 mm wide with BACKWARD-POINTING microscopic teeth along both edges.
Open terminal/axillary panicles often have 2 or more branches at the lowest nodes (important contrast with Leersia virginica).
Narrow 4–6.5 mm flattened one-flowered spikelets, glumes absent or inconspicuous.
Rhizomes often long, with scales not closely overlapping.
crew_field_check: Handle rough edges carefully with lens/forceps; don't deliberately drag fingers along the blade.
Check exact same plant for 2+ basal panicle branches and 4–6.5 mm narrow mature spikelet.
Separate 1-flowered Leersia with obscure glumes from similar wetland grasses and related cutgrasses.
Don't claim species by habitat alone; capture collar and rhizome only if visible.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: WHOLE: same rooted stand in shallow water/creek margin; multiple branches attached to base, habitat in frame.
LEAF MARGIN: strong 10× macro with 1 mm reference showing tiny DOWNWARD/RETRORSE sharp hairs or teeth; avoid running bare fingers along the edge.
TRUE LIGULE: junction of blade and sheath, roughly 0.5–1.5 mm short membranous edge with scale.
SHEATH / NODE: rough sheath surface and any small bands of hairs at attached stem nodes.
PANICLE: clearly show 2 or more branches from the LOWEST main flowering-head node, if present; contrast with white cutgrass single branch.
SPIKELET: 4–6.5 mm narrow compressed unit against millimeter scale, both faces and glume-free base/attachment shown.
RHIZOME: exposed long creeping underground stem with spaced non-overlapping scales, only where collecting is allowed; restore exposed soil.
OPTIONAL: reduced upper sheath-enclosed axillary flowerhead (cleistogamous panicle), if found on same plant.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Rice cutgrass L. oryzoides: notably retrorse-prickly/rough leaves and sheaths; mature spreading panicle usually 2+ branches at lowermost nodes (verify their COMMON point on rachis); oblong flat 1-flowered spikelets usually 4.2–6.5 × 1.3–1.7 mm and short membranous ligule 0.5–1 mm. White cutgrass L. virginica: usually smoother or less harshly rough sheaths, often a single panicle branch at a lowermost node, smaller more crowded/overlapping spikelets ~2.2–4 mm; count mature branching and measure spikelets rather than rely on roughness. L. lenticularis has wider, almost disk- or lens-shaped spikelets, not narrow 'rice grains'. Zizaniopsis and Zizania have different flowering structure; Texas wild-rice is a protected aquatic plant and must not be handled or uprooted for comparisons. Paspalum spikelets are generally arranged differently; inspect the actual glumes/lemmas, not just habitat.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Usually more delicate with smoother or only moderately rough leaf sheaths. Flowering head generally has ONE branch at a low node rather than two or more; small spikelets (~2.4–4 mm) often crowded/overlapping more strongly; short closely overlapping rhizome scales. Mature paired-branch and spikelet counts are more reliable than wet habitat alone.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Whole panicle lower branching node and single spikelet with mm reference; correct source-labelled specimen.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Spikelets are broad and round or lens-shaped rather than elongate narrow 'rice grains'; may be nearly circular and often look like little disks. Large leaf blades may be similarly rough, so seek mature spikelet dimensions and outline.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Spikelets from face and edge, with mm ruler and attached pedicel.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Much taller robust marsh grass with broad blades and a large branching panicle whose reproductive spikelets are organized differently; compare whole plant scale and flowering structures, not sharp leaf edges alone.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Whole stand and size comparison plus panicle close-up.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Aquatic perennial from flowing river channels with dramatically different pollen- and seed-bearing branches. Do not mistake any narrow water-edge grass leaf for this endangered localized aquatic grass. Species diagnosis and stewardship need the actual inflorescence and habitat context.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Legal non-disturbing habitat and clear flowering anatomy; never uproot protected wild-rice.

detailed_pairs.field_split: Many one-sided racemes bear two-flowered spikelets and a membranous ligule. Leersia typically has very rough leaf surfaces/margins, more flexible open panicle branches, and flattened one-flowered spikelets with no evident glumes.
detailed_pairs.photo_need: Matched leaf-edge and flowering branch + single spikelet macro.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: LOOK AT THE EDGES OF THE LEAVES (CAREFULLY): rice cutgrass has extremely ROUGH, backward-pointing sharp microscopic teeth on blade margins and often sheaths. In wetland stands it makes open branching panicles of small flattened grain-like one-flowered spikelets (often ~4–6 mm), with very short membranous true ligule. For L. oryzoides versus white cutgrass, compare the LOWEST panicle node (often 2 or more branches) and measured mature spikelets; do not identify by roughness alone.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Rice cutgrass — 5-photo crew check (do not use your bare fingers on the serrated edge)
steps: Find a wet-site plant with a clearly attached flowering head and photograph the whole clump and stem from ground to panicle; current photos show flowerhead portions, NOT a traced rooted plant.

Check the LEAF EDGE using macro and backlight: tiny retrorse (backward-pointing) spinules along the edge and rough sheath, with a 1-mm scale. This is the hallmark missing photo; never feel across the blade with bare skin.

Photograph the LOWEST panicle branching node with the central axis and ALL departing primary branches in focus. Rice cutgrass typically has 2 or more at this node; no existing arrow demonstrates this.

Put a mature spikelet under 10–20× alongside a millimeter rule: narrow flattened one-flowered unit typically ~4.2–6.5 mm; inspect its awnless profile and reduced/absent true glumes, not individual structures guessed from a hand-scale photo.

Open a FRESH blade–sheath junction for the 0.5–1 mm membranous ligule. Compare source-identified white cutgrass's often single lower branch and smaller spikelets, and disk-like catchfly cutgrass. Photograph without damaging protected wetland grasses.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Leaf-edge retrorse prickles + mature open panicle + typically 2+ branches at basal PANICLE nodes + narrow measured 4.2–6.5 mm spikelets strongly support L. oryzoides; no single one proves the species.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Photo 2's broad leaves may belong to neighboring grass stems, not necessarily the photographed Leersia culm. Neither archived photo shows microscopic leaf teeth, a definite 2+ lowermost branch origin, actual glumeless base, a measured ligule or a rooted rhizome. Original Joey study-only photo is not silently licensed by unrelated footage permission. Avoid touching sharp leaf edges with bare hands.
